title: The Club Filter and the Nonstationary Ideal
description: Answers the first open question of CantorDiagonalizationOQ02OQ03OQ02 (Fodor's pressing-down lemma): formalize the club filter on a regular uncountable cardinal κ and identify the stationary sets as exactly the sets not in its dual ideal. Proves that the whole space is a club, that the intersection of two clubs is a club (with the genuine content — unboundedness — established by interleaving the two clubs into a single ω-chain whose supremum is approached cofinally from inside each club), and by induction that any finite intersection of clubs is a club. Defines the nonstationary ideal (sets disjoint from some club), proves it is downward closed, closed under finite unions (using the binary club-intersection theorem), proper, and that a set is stationary iff it is not nonstationary. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext:
The club filter and its dual, the nonstationary ideal, are among the most fundamental objects of combinatorial set theory. For a regular uncountable cardinal κ, the closed unbounded (club) subsets of the ordinals below κ are closed under finite — in fact κ-sized diagonal — intersection, and so generate a proper, κ-complete filter Club(κ). The sets that meet every club are the stationary sets; the sets disjoint from some club form the nonstationary ideal NS(κ), the dual of Club(κ).

The basic finite theory goes back to the same circle of ideas as Fodor's 1956 pressing-down lemma: the parent proof CantorDiagonalizationOQ02OQ03OQ02 formalized Fodor's lemma using the diagonal intersection of κ clubs. That development left the elementary filter/ideal bookkeeping — that two clubs already intersect in a club, that finite intersections stay clubs, and that stationarity is exactly non-membership in the dual ideal — as its first open question. This file discharges it.

The binary intersection theorem (Jech, Set Theory, Theorem 8.3) is the historical entry point to the whole subject: it is the first nontrivial sign that clubs behave like a filter of 'large' sets, and its proof — interleaving two clubs into one increasing ω-sequence and using closedness at the supremum — is the simplest instance of the diagonalization that the parent proof carried out at full κ-indexed generality.
overview.problemStatement: Let κ be a regular uncountable cardinal and work with subsets of the ordinals below κ.ord. A club is a closed unbounded set; the club filter Club(κ) is generated by the clubs and its dual ideal is the nonstationary ideal NS(κ) (sets disjoint from some club). Show that (i) clubs are closed under finite intersection (so Club(κ) is a filter) with the whole space as top and ∅ excluded (properness), and (ii) the stationary sets — those meeting every club — are exactly the sets not in NS(κ).
overview.proofStrategy:
Two strands.

Filter side: The whole space is a club because κ.ord is a limit ordinal (closed trivially, unbounded by α ↦ α+1). The crux is binary intersection. Closedness of C ∩ D is immediate (cofinality in the intersection forces cofinality in each factor). For unboundedness, given α₀ build a single ω-chain by alternately stepping into C and then into D: pick c₀ ∈ C above α₀, d₀ ∈ D above c₀, c₁ ∈ C above d₀, and so on. Regularity bounds the supremum γ below κ.ord (iSup_lt_ord_lift_of_isRegular). The C-points cₙ are cofinal in γ, so closedness of C gives γ ∈ C; the D-points dₙ are cofinal in γ, so γ ∈ D; hence γ ∈ C ∩ D above α₀. Finite intersection then follows by induction on a Finset of indices.

Ideal side: Define NS(κ) by 'disjoint from some club'. Downward closure under ⊆ reuses the same avoiding club. Closure under binary union is exactly where the binary intersection theorem is needed: if S avoids the club C and T avoids the club D, then S ∪ T avoids the club C ∩ D. The empty set is nonstationary (avoided by the whole space), and the whole space is stationary (every club is nonempty by unboundedness at 0 < κ.ord), so Club(κ) is proper. Finally, S is stationary iff ¬ ∃ club disjoint from S, which is precisely ¬ IsNonStationary κ S.
keyInsights: Two clubs already intersect in a club — no diagonalization over κ indices is needed; the binary case is just the interleaving of two cofinal sequences into one.

The single ω-chain α₀ < c₀ < d₀ < c₁ < d₁ < ⋯ carries TWO cofinal subsequences below its supremum γ: the cₙ ∈ C and the dₙ ∈ D. Closedness applied separately to each factor puts γ in both, which is the whole trick.

Closure of the nonstationary ideal under finite unions is the dual face of closure of the club filter under finite intersections: S∪T avoids C∩D. This is the precise structural link between the two theorems and shows why the filter property is exactly what the ideal needs.

Stationarity is definitionally the negation of ideal membership: 'meets every club' is the De Morgan dual of 'disjoint from some club', so isStationary_iff_not_isNonStationary is a clean double-negation identity rather than new mathematics — the content lives in the filter/ideal closure theorems.

Regularity is used only for unboundedness, never for closedness: inter_isClosedBelow is a purely topological fact about closed sets that needs no hypothesis on κ at all, while inter_isUnbounded's single appeal to iSup_lt_ord_lift_of_isRegular is exactly where 'κ regular' earns its keep — it guarantees an ω-indexed supremum of ordinals below κ stays below κ. This fails for singular κ: if κ = ℵ_ω, whose cofinality is ω, a countable increasing sequence of ordinals below κ can have supremum κ itself, so the interleaving construction would not close up inside κ.ord.
prerequisites: ordinal arithmetic and suprema (iSup of an ℕ-indexed family of ordinals)

sections.title: File Header and Overview
sections.content: Module documentation stating the open question being answered, the five results (club top, binary intersection, finite intersection, the nonstationary ideal, duality), and references (Jech §8 Theorem 8.3, Kunen Ch. II §6). Imports Mathlib and the parent file Proofs.CantorDiagonalizationOQ02OQ03OQ02, reusing its IsClub / IsStationary / IsUnboundedBelow / IsClosedBelow definitions and not_isStationary_iff; opens namespace FodorLemma with Cardinal Order Ordinal Set.

sections.title: §1. The Whole Space is a Club
sections.content: isClub_univ: Set.univ is a club. Closed trivially; unbounded because κ.ord is a successor-limit (isSuccLimit_ord from κ ≥ ℵ₀), so α ↦ α+1 stays below κ.ord. This is the top element of the club filter.

sections.title: §2. Intersection of Two Clubs is Closed
sections.content: inter_isClosedBelow: the easy half. A point cofinal in C ∩ D is cofinal in C and in D separately, so closedness of each factor places it in both.

sections.title: §3. Intersection of Two Clubs is Unbounded
sections.content: inter_isUnbounded: the genuine content. From α₀ the proof builds a single increasing ω-chain via Choice: cElt steps into C above the current point, dElt steps into D above that c; the recursion seq carries the proof that each term is < κ.ord. The supremum γ = ⨆ s is < κ.ord by iSup_lt_ord_lift_of_isRegular. The cElt-values are cofinal in γ giving γ ∈ C (closedness of C), and the s(n+1) = dElt-values are cofinal in γ giving γ ∈ D, so γ ∈ C ∩ D lies above α₀.

sections.title: §3 (cont). Binary Intersection is a Club
sections.content: inter_isClub: combines the closed and unbounded halves — the club filter is closed under binary intersection.

sections.title: §4. Finite Intersection of Clubs is a Club
sections.content: isClub_biInter: by Finset induction, ⋂ i ∈ t, C i is a club. Empty case is isClub_univ; the insert case rewrites via Finset.set_biInter_insert and applies inter_isClub. This is the defining filter-closure property.

sections.title: §5. The Nonstationary Ideal and Duality
sections.content: IsNonStationary κ S := ∃ club C disjoint from S (the dual ideal NS(κ)). isStationary_iff_not_isNonStationary: stationary ⟺ not nonstationary (via not_isStationary_iff). isNonStationary_subset (downward closed), isNonStationary_union (closed under ∪, using inter_isClub on the two avoiding clubs), isNonStationary_empty (∅ ∈ NS), and isStationary_univ (the whole space is stationary, so Club(κ) is proper).

sections.title: §6. Implications and Mathematical Notes
sections.content: The finite filter/ideal theory underpins the σ-complete (indeed κ-complete) club filter. The binary intersection theorem is the base case of the κ-indexed diagonal-intersection theorem the parent used for Fodor's lemma; closure of NS(κ) under finite unions is the dual statement. Natural next steps: κ-completeness of the club filter (countable / <κ intersections), the normality of NS(κ) via the diagonal intersection, and Solovay's stationary-set splitting.

conclusion.summary: This file formalizes the finite theory of the club filter Club(κ) and the nonstationary ideal NS(κ) on a regular uncountable cardinal κ, answering the first open question of the parent Fodor's-lemma proof. It proves that the whole space is a club, that the intersection of two clubs is a club (the unbounded half via interleaving two clubs into one ω-chain), and by induction that finite intersections of clubs are clubs — establishing that the clubs generate a proper filter. Dually, it defines NS(κ) as the sets disjoint from some club, proves NS(κ) is downward closed, closed under finite unions (using binary club-intersection), proper, and that a set is stationary exactly when it is not nonstationary. 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications:
**Club filter as a filter of large sets**: Finite intersection closure plus properness is exactly the statement that Club(κ) is a proper filter; the stationary sets are its 'positive' sets and NS(κ) is its dual ideal. This is the finite backbone of the κ-complete club filter used throughout combinatorial set theory.

**Duality with the parent**: The binary intersection theorem is the base case of the parent's κ-indexed diagonal-intersection theorem (diagInter_isClub). Closure of NS(κ) under finite unions is its dual face. Together they make the filter/ideal language in which Fodor's lemma — 'a regressive function on a stationary set is constant on a stationary set' — is naturally stated.

**Toward normality**: With finite closure in place, the natural continuations are κ-completeness (<κ-sized intersections of clubs are clubs, again via diagInter) and normality of NS(κ) (closure under diagonal unions), the property that makes the nonstationary ideal the canonical normal ideal on κ.
openQuestions: Prove κ-completeness of the club filter directly in this filter language: the intersection of fewer than κ clubs is a club (the parent's diagInter_isClub gives the κ-indexed diagonal version; deduce the genuine <κ-intersection statement and the dual <κ-union closure of NS(κ)).

Formalize normality of the nonstationary ideal: if each Sᵦ ∈ NS(κ) then the diagonal union {α | ∃ β < α, α ∈ Sᵦ} ∈ NS(κ), equivalently the diagonal intersection of clubs is a club restated for the ideal — making NS(κ) a normal ideal and recovering Fodor's lemma as the statement that NS(κ) is normal.
